# About NHANES dataset
Throughout our past assignments, we have regularly used a cleaned_NHANES dataset. This dataset was selected from *The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey* (NHANES) data. It includes the blood pressure data and demographic data collected during three NHANES survey cycles: 

* 2013-2014: [@nhanes_2013_2014]
* 2015-2016: [@nhanes_2015_2016]
* 2017-2018: [@nhanes_2017_2018]

This dataset has been cleaned and is provided as "cleaned_NHANES.csv". It contains 29,400 observations and has 21 different variables (some in character and others in integers).

Below, we will follow through a brief description of a couple of variables from the dataset, presented into two tables. The required packages and data are loaded and imported  as such:


## Load packages and data import
```{r package and data}
library(pacman)
pacman::p_load(rio, here, dplyr, gtsummary,
               forcats, kableExtra)

# Data import
cleaned_NHANES <- import(here("Data", "cleaned_NHANES.csv"))
```

# Data description

As mentioned previously about the selected data from NHANES, we worked on data from 3 survey cycles. We will therefore be comparing between survey cycles (also called waves) different statistical information for a couple of variables.

In the first table, seen below, we have compared for each wave ID, the numbers and percentage of males, and of ethnicity category.

## General statsitical overview per wave for sex and ethnicity variables

```{r table1, echo = FALSE}

variables_table <- cleaned_NHANES %>%
  mutate(ethnicity_2 = fct_infreq(ethnicity_2)) %>%
  select(wave_id, gender, ethnicity_2) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = wave_id,
    type = gender ~ "dichotomous",
    value = gender ~ "Male",
    statistic = all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)",
    sort = ethnicity_2 ~ "frequency",
    label = list(gender ~ "Male", ethnicity_2 ~ "Ethnicity")
  )

#adding extra for readability
variables_table <- variables_table %>%
    modify_header(
    label ~ "**Wave ID**",
    all_stat_cols() ~ "**{level}** \nN = {n}"
    ) %>%
  as_kable_extra(
    booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "",
    caption = "Sex and ethnicity description of NHANES participants by wave"
    ) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position", "scale_down"))

variables_table

```

Using the table above, we first observe a similar percentage of males for each wave, despite decreasing overall sample size of each wave.
In addition to this, there seems to also be a general similarity of ethnicity proportion between waves.

Considering that all three waves are relatively similar in sex proportions and in ethnicity diversity proportions, we will follow with a statistical description of the average Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) for each wave.

## Average SBP statistical summary per wave

Below we find Table 2, presenting a summary of the average Systolic Blood Pressure per wave.

```{r average SBP, echo = FALSE}
# recreating average SBP because it had been created on a separate filtered dataset


#creating one dataframe with all the SBP values 
SBP_df <- data.frame (
  SBP1 = cleaned_NHANES$systolic_bp_1,
  SBP2 = cleaned_NHANES$systolic_bp_2,
  SBP3 = cleaned_NHANES$systolic_bp_3,
  SBP4 = cleaned_NHANES$systolic_bp_4
)

# making a SBP average, despite NA missing data
SBP_average <- rowMeans(SBP_df, na.rm = TRUE)

cleaned_NHANES <- cleaned_NHANES %>%
  mutate(
    SBP_average = SBP_average
  )
# Set SBP_mean to NA if all 4 values are missing
cleaned_NHANES$SBP_average[
  is.nan(cleaned_NHANES$SBP_average)] <- NA
```

```{r table2, echo = FALSE}
SBP_table <- cleaned_NHANES %>%
  select(wave_id, SBP_average) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = wave_id,
    type = SBP_average ~ "continuous2",
    statistic = SBP_average ~ c(
      "{min}",
      "{max}",
      "{median}",
      "{mean}",
      "{sd}"
    ),
    digits = SBP_average ~ 1,
    label = list(SBP_average ~ "Average Systolic Blood Pressure (mmHg)"),
    missing = "ifany"
  )

## adding footnote:

SBP_table <- SBP_table %>%
    modify_header(
    label ~ "**Wave ID**",
    all_stat_cols() ~ "**{level}** \nN = {n}"
    ) %>%
  as_kable_extra(
    booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "",
    caption = "Average systolic blood pressure by wave") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position", "scale_down")) %>%
  footnote(
    general = "SD = standard deviation.",
    general_title = "Note:",
    footnote_as_chunk = TRUE
  )

SBP_table

```

The table above allows us to observe the evolution of the average SBP throughout time for the general population of the United-States.

It is interesting to notice that, despite decrease of overall sample size and of missing values (see Unknown), there seems to be a **general increase** in the statistics of the average SBP.
Indeed, we notice this by comparing values of each row for each survey cycle. In the span of 3 survey cycle (2014-2018):

* Min: **augmented** from 64.7 to 72.7 **(+8)**
* Max: **augmented** from 228.7 to 234.0 **(+5.3)**
* Median: **augmented** from 115.3 to 118.0 **(+2.7)**
* Mean: **augmented** from 118.3 to 121.7 **(+3.4)**
* Standard deviation (SD): **augmented** from 18.1 to 20.3 **(+2.2)**

Though this simple observation of data statistics is not complete enough to confirm this observed trend, let alone explain it, it is a first step to point out potential research that could further the understanding of this data.

End
